title: Why do the last digits decide divisibility by four and eight?
description: The video explains with place values why four needs only the last two digits and eight only the last three. It then uses the shortcuts on three thousand seven hundred sixteen and fifty one thousand two hundred forty.
teaching_notes: One idea: a divisor divides every place value from some place upward, so only the digits below that place are left to test. Watch for students who test the whole number, or only the units digit, instead of the last two or three digits.

source: Checking Divisibility Quickly: the shortcuts for 4 and 8
video_script.why: The student has seen that ten divides every place value except the units place and now finds where four and eight begin to divide every place value.
video_script.substitution: Find the place value from which the divisor divides every place, then test only the digits below that place.
video_script.anchor: a chart of place values, with the places that the divisor divides marked and the last digits left to test
video_script.payoff_line: Four needs the last two digits and eight needs the last three

final_answer.value: 4 needs the last two digits and 8 the last three; 3716 is divisible by 4 and 51240 by 8
final_answer.spoken: four needs the last two digits and eight the last three, and three thousand seven hundred sixteen is divisible by four and fifty one thousand two hundred forty by eight

maths_rules: 100 = 4 x 25, so every place value from the hundreds up is a multiple of 4
a number is divisible by 4 exactly when the number made by its last two digits is divisible by 4
1000 = 8 x 125, so every place value from the thousands up is a multiple of 8
a number is divisible by 8 exactly when the number made by its last three digits is divisible by 8
3716 ends in 16 = 4 x 4, so 3716 is divisible by 4
51240 ends in 240 = 8 x 30, so 51240 is divisible by 8
